Orchot Tzadikim 4:2: Insolence is a trait that is bad in most of its effects, and it is the opposite of the trait of shame. For the shame-filled person overlooks the wrongs done to him, and has compassion, and pardons, and forgives; but whoever is insolent ("brazen-faced") is not ashamed before any man, but stands with insolence toward everyone, and does every evil deed without shame, but rather strengthens himself in his wickedness and hardens himself in transgression. Of this it is said (Jeremiah 5:3), "they have made their faces harder than rock," and it is said (Ezekiel 2:4), "and the children are impudent and hard-hearted."
Orchot Tzadikim 4:3: And all the good qualities said of shame are the opposite in insolence. And when a person grows powerful in this trait, he becomes very despicable in people's eyes, even if he is a wise man. And many evils follow from insolence, for whoever brazens his face toward people cannot escape strife, hatred, and envy. And whoever is brazen-faced denies his lineage (Yevamot 79a); he will show no deference to a great man, nor show favor to an elder, and all the transgressions in the Torah become light in his eyes to commit, all according to the degree of insolence within him. And of him it is said (Avot 5:20): brazenness of face leads to Gehinnom.
Orchot Tzadikim 4:4: The insolent man is called "wicked," as it is said (Proverbs 21:29), "a wicked man hardens his face." And the wicked are disgraceful and repulsive before the Blessed Lord, and the name of the wicked is disgraceful, as it is written (ibid. 10:7), "and the name of the wicked shall rot." Of shame it is said (Psalms 25:9), "and He teaches the humble His way"; but of the brazen wicked man it is said (ibid. 146:9), "but the way of the wicked He makes crooked."
Orchot Tzadikim 4:5: Whoever has the trait of insolence commits transgressions bundle upon bundle and regards himself as righteous. It is against this way of thinking that we confess: "we are not so brazen-faced and stiff-necked as to say before You, Lord our God, that we are righteous and have not sinned, but rather we and our fathers have sinned." And it is a very sick and bad trait for a wicked man to say, "I have not sinned," and for this the Holy One, blessed be He, judges him and has no mercy on him, as it is written (Jeremiah 2:35), "behold, I will enter into judgment with you, because you say, I have not sinned"; and it is written (Proverbs 28:13), "but he who confesses and forsakes [his sins] shall find mercy." And this brazen path is very far from the ways of teshuvah. And of the harlot it is said (ibid. 7:13), "she made her face brazen and said to him." This trait is very bad, for it brings a person to shame his fellow and to shame the poor, as the matter is stated (ibid. 18:23), "the poor man speaks pleadingly, but the rich man answers harshly." How much more so if he shames his teachers and brazens his face against them, and hardens his neck against those who rebuke him, out of the greatness of his insolence — then this trait removes him from the world. And it is fitting to keep it far from one's soul.
Orchot Tzadikim 4:6: But this trait is very praiseworthy when it is insolence for the sake of Torah and divine service: to brazen one's face against the wicked, and to harden one's neck against them, so as not to listen to their counsel, and not to concede to their falsehoods and abominations, and not to flatter them. And one must brazen his face even in the fulfillment of the commandments, even if people mock him for it. And one must brazen his face before his teachers, to ask what he does not know, and not be ashamed of this (Avot 3:5). And one must brazen his face to rebuke people, to expose their sins to them.
Orchot Tzadikim 4:7: And a person must uphold this trait carefully: to suppress it where it is disgraceful, and to overcome it with all his strength. For it is very difficult to escape this bad trait, unless one applies the full force of his power and the might of his strength, to conquer it and turn it away from himself in a place of sin, while establishing it within himself and upon his face in a place where he receives reward for hardness of neck.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:2: Love encompasses more actions than any other trait. And when a person directs his love toward evil, there is no trait as bad as it among all traits; and when a person directs his love toward good, it is above all traits, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:5), "and you shall love the Lord your God" — and there is no higher level in the service of the Creator than that of one who serves out of love.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:3: And now hear how love corrupts deeds, when a person lets his love overpower his wisdom. For there are several kinds of love, each different from the next. The first love: a person loves his children, and out of the greatness of his love he does not discipline them or guide them to a good path, but lets them go according to the wantonness of their evil heart — and from this great harm will come.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:4: The second love: love of money. And out of the greatness of his longing for money, his business dealings will not be conducted with faithfulness, and he will covet, oppress, and rob in order to increase his wealth; and out of the greatness of his craving for riches, he will close his hand from charity, and be narrow of eye.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:5: The third love: love of women. And if he has a bad wife, given to pride, she will remove all the commandments from his heart, and will draw him after her; and out of the greatness of his love he will not brazen his face against her, but will listen to her counsel, and she will bring him to bad conduct. And also, out of the greatness of his love of women, he will gaze at them constantly, and will come to adultery.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:6: The fourth love is love of one's relatives: one's father and mother, brothers and sisters and other relatives, and one's friends and companions. And out of love for them he will assist them in their disputes, and will not scrutinize whether they have wronged those they dispute with; rather, he will always help and shield and cover for them, and even if they have committed many breaches, he will shield them. And he will also listen to their counsel, and even if that counsel is not good, he will not depart from their words. And he will also wish to raise them to positions unsuited to them, such as making them rulers and leaders of the generation and having them rule over the people, and even if they are wicked he will not be concerned about this. And behold, love blinds his eyes and deafens his ears, and there is great corruption in this, for they will mislead the people into their own vanities.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:7: The fifth love is love of long life. And out of the greatness of his love of life, he will not stand firm through a trial.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:8: The sixth love is love of honor. And whoever loves honor, his deeds will not be for the sake of Heaven, for in all the commandments he performs — whether he gives charity, or occupies himself with Torah, or with other commandments — his thought and his intent will be after praise and honor, desiring that people give him honor and greatness. And this is a great loss in the performance of divine service, and even one who has Torah and good deeds — honor removes him from the world; how much more so one who has neither Torah nor good deeds, and pursues honor, for then how many of his deeds become disgraceful.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:9: And there is yet a seventh love, which is worse than all loves, and it is love of pleasures and indulgences: such as eating and drinking, and other pleasures such as lewdness and outings. And there is no need to elaborate on this matter, for one who loves wine and becomes drunk, and constantly eats delicacies, and goes regularly to the house of feasting — he will forget his Maker, as it is written (Deuteronomy 21:15-16 — actually 32:15), "and you shall eat and be satisfied; take heed to yourselves, lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve..."; and it is written (ibid. 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:10: Whoever wishes to escape the snare of the fowler that is all these loves needs great wisdom and much courage, lest he be caught in their corruption. For all these loves surround a person's heart, and if he pushes away one or two loves from within him, the remaining loves will still pursue him from light into darkness. Therefore you must be taught to be careful and diligent in making use of all these loves, to come to know through them the ways of the Blessed Lord, as the matter is stated (Proverbs 3:6), "in all your ways know Him."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:11: Love of one's children should be along this path: that he think of guiding his children in the ways of justice, and teaching them the practice of the service of the Blessed Lord, and commanding them after him to serve the Blessed Lord, as the matter is stated (Isaiah 38:19), "the father shall make known Your truth to the children"; and it is written (Deuteronomy 4:9), "and you shall make them known to your children and your children's children." And as it is said of Abraham (Genesis 18:19), "for I have known him, that he will command his children and his household after him."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:12: And love of money should be along this path: he should love his money so that he not covet the money of others, and not need to steal or rob; and not need to receive charity, but rather sustain others from his own; and clothe and feed the poor, and use his money to support students of Torah who fear the Lord. And also, because of his wealth, he should free himself from the affairs of this world, and set aside times for Torah study and for fulfilling the commandments, since he has the means to do so; and he should not trust in the abundance of his wealth so as to become proud, but rather should use his perishable wealth to purchase the life of the World to Come, which does not perish. In this way he should love his money.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:13: And love of women should be along this path: that he think that she saves him from sin and keeps him far from adultery, and through her he fulfills the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying, and she raises his children. And she serves him all her days, and prepares his food and the other needs of the household; and through this he is free to study Torah and occupy himself with the commandments, and she helps him in the service of the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:14: And love of his father and mother should be along this path: that he think that they raised him, and toiled over him to teach him the ways of the Blessed Lord, and instructed and educated him in Torah and commandments. And through them he fulfills the commandment of the Blessed Creator, as it is written (Exodus 20:12), "honor your father and your mother."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:15: And he should love his brothers and sisters and other relatives along this path: that they occupy themselves in bringing him to good qualities, and they assist him in the service of the Blessed Creator. And he in turn should occupy himself with them, to teach them and rebuke them, and show them no undue favor — and in this there is reward for him, and it is a great trait, as it is written (Psalms 15:3), "nor takes up reproach against his kinsman."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:16: And a person derives much benefit from his relatives, as we find with Lot, whom Abraham rescued and fought for; and he was also saved in Sodom by the merit of Abraham.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:17: And he should love his friends and all the rest of Israel with a complete love, in order to fulfill what is said (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your fellow as yourself." And this is a great principle in the Torah: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow (Shabbat 31a). And greater than this is (Genesis 9:6), "for in the image of God He made man" (Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:6).
Orchot Tzadikim 5:18: And there is great benefit for whoever conducts himself with affection and friendship toward people —
Orchot Tzadikim 5:19: one benefit in this world, and a second for the World to Come. The benefit of this world: whoever conducts himself with love toward every person, everyone will help him. If he falls, his helpers and supporters will be many; and if someone stands against him to contend with him, many will stand by him to save him. And if people speak ill of him, many will silence those speaking ill and put them to shame. And if trouble comes upon him, everyone will grieve for him and lend him a hand. And if he comes to distress and poverty, many will show him mercy by giving him gifts.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:20: The benefit for the World to Come: because he is beloved by all, his words are heeded, and he has the power to rebuke people so that they improve their deeds. And also, through this love he lives at peace with everyone, and through this he is calm and at ease, and free to study Torah and do good deeds. And also through this love people will help him, doing his work and shielding him, and he will find much more room to serve the Blessed Creator with a complete service. And because of this love he finds favor in the eyes of all who see him, and his good deeds will be accepted by all, and each person will desire to do as he does.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:21: And by what path does a person attain love of every other person? I shall instruct you and teach you:
Orchot Tzadikim 5:22: The path is that he help every person with his person and with his money, according to his ability.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:23: Helping with his person means that he serve every person, whether poor or rich, and exert himself on their behalf.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:24: Helping with his money means that he lend to the rich man when he needs funds, and likewise lend to the poor man in his time of distress, and likewise give him gifts according to his own means, and at certain times send gifts and presents even to the rich. And he should be generous with what is his. If he has dealings with people, all his business should be conducted with faithfulness, and he should not be exacting with his fellow over a small matter. He should always wish that his fellow benefit from him, and not strive to benefit from his fellow. His words should always be gentle toward people: if someone shames him, he should not shame him back; if someone deceives him, he should not deceive him back. He should bear upon his own neck the yoke of the world, and not burden others with it. He should not quarrel with anyone, and should receive every person with joy and a pleasant countenance, for a pleasant countenance strengthens love. He should deal with his fellow for his fellow's benefit, and comfort every person in his grief and worry. If someone reveals a secret to him, he should not reveal it, even if that person angers him. He should speak evil of no one, and should not listen to others speaking evil of anyone. He should always strive to find merit in people wherever possible, and be all the more careful in this — and then he will be beloved by all. He should honor every person in his deeds and his words. He should not be proud toward anyone, but should submit under every person. And in all his deeds he should direct his intent toward Heaven. And he must be very careful of the company of unworthy people, so as not to learn from their deeds, and to stay far from the company of scoffers.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:25: And the wise man said to his son: hear, my son! When it occurs to you to associate with people, associate with a wise man, as it is written (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise"; and it is said (ibid. 9:9), "give to a wise man, and he will grow still wiser." For if you grow wise, he will glorify you and not dispute your wisdom, and then you will know that you can rely on your own wisdom. If you honor him, he will honor you; if you show him respect, he will show you respect; and if you need his help, he will help you; and whatever you say, he will affirm; if you become angry, he will bear with you; and you will learn from his good deeds. And associate with every person from whom you can learn things that will bring you to the service of the Blessed Creator. And our Sages said: when you wish to associate with someone, provoke him to anger, and if he admits the truth to you even in his anger, associate with him; and if not, leave him be. And associate only with one who recognizes his own worth, for whoever does not recognize his own worth — there is no benefit in his company. Acquire for yourself a friend who rebukes you when you act improperly, and who teaches you to do good, and do not grow weary of his rebuke; and one who helps you with his person and his money — acquire such a helper and do not let him go, for this is your true friend. But a friend who flatters you, and who straightens out your errors and mistakes for you [rather than correcting you], and comforts you over your bad deeds — remove yourself from him, and keep your foot far from his path.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:26: And likewise a friend who takes what he needs from you, and causes you great harm for a small benefit to himself — hasten to turn away from him. And do not associate with those who agree upon wrongdoing, as it is said (Isaiah 8:12), "do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:27: And it is forbidden to associate with a wicked man in worldly dealings, as it is said (2 Chronicles 20:37), "because you have associated with Ahaziah, the Lord has made a breach in your works."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:28: And even for the sake of a commandment it is forbidden to associate with a wicked man, as it is said (Proverbs 3:31), "do not envy a man of violence, and choose none of his ways." And our Sages said in Avot d'Rabbi Natan (9:4): keep far from a bad neighbor, and do not associate with a wicked man even for the sake of a commandment, for the ways of death found in the company of the wicked are many.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:29: And if a person is exacting with himself, and his words are gentle with his fellow creatures, and his mind is at ease among them; if he is insulted and does not insult back, and honors even those who demean him, and conducts his dealings with faithfulness, and does not spend much time in the company and gatherings of the ignorant masses, and is always seen occupied with Torah, wrapped in tzitzit and crowned with tefillin, and does all his deeds beyond the strict letter of the law — provided he does not go so far in this as to become strange or estranged — until everyone comes to praise him and love him and desire to emulate his deeds — behold, this one has sanctified the Name, and of him the verse says (Isaiah 49:3), "and He said to me, you are My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:30: And love of long life should be along this path: that he love the days of his life not in order to eat and drink and indulge himself in his fleeting days, but rather that he think: the work of Torah and commandments is so vast that even if I were to live twice as long, or many times over, I could not complete the requirement of the Torah and attain the virtues of the Torah, by which a servant becomes pleasing to his master. Along this path he should love the days of his life, for through them he acquires the service of the Blessed Creator, and pure fear of Him, and love of Him, and acquires provisions in this world that will carry him into the World to Come; and in this world and these fleeting days he acquires the world that endures — a delight that will never cease, forever and ever. And he should constantly fear death, lest he has not yet reached the fullest perfection he is capable of reaching, and every single day he should add love and fear of the Omnipresent.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:31: But a life without the fear of the Lord is not called "life," and one should feel disgust and loathing for a life that stands against the Blessed Creator, as the matter is said of Rebecca (Genesis 27:46), "I am disgusted with my life because of the daughters of Heth; if Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth like these, from the daughters of the land, what good is life to me?" And therefore, wherever there is desecration of the Name, he should not concern himself over his own life, and his heart should always be ready to give himself over for the sanctification of the Name in all the commandments, both the light ones and the grave ones.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:32: Love of honor is very bad; therefore let a person distance himself from honor with all his ability. And if a person distances himself from two things — honor and benefiting from others — he is then close to all the good virtues. For honor corrupts all deeds, since in every deed he performs he will think of gaining honor for himself. And even if he does not concern himself with honor, if he pursues benefiting from others, then all his deeds are corrupted, for his heart will always be inclined after gain. Therefore let him take to heart to distance himself from honor, and also from benefiting from others.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:33: But sometimes there is a commandment in pursuing honor, such as when a man is righteous and wise, and people belittle him and mock him because of his good deeds, and through this his words are held in contempt and are not heeded — and if he has the power to compel people to honor him and heed his rebukes and his words, then in such a case one should pursue honor in order to rebuke people. For instance, if he was disgraced in public, he should not forgive until they appease him. But most of the time he should withdraw from honor and flee from it. Have not our Sages said (Avot 4:21): envy, desire, and honor remove a person from the world. He should not study nor do any good deed in order to be honored, but should do the good deed for the sake of the Blessed Creator, and honor will come in the end.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:34: Love of pleasures, such as eating, drinking, and sleep: know that a person must direct all his deeds toward knowing the Blessed Lord, and his sitting and his rising and his speech should all correspond to this one purpose. How so? When he conducts business, or does any deed or work, he should not have in his heart the mere accumulation of money alone; rather, he should do these things in order to obtain the things the body needs — food, drink, dwelling in a home, and marrying a wife. And when he eats and drinks and has marital relations, he should not set his heart on these things for the sake of pleasure alone, to the point that he is found eating and drinking only what is sweet to the palate, and having relations only for pleasure; rather, he should set his heart on eating in order to nourish his body and his limbs. Therefore he should not eat everything the palate craves, like the dog and the donkey, but should eat things that benefit the body, whether bitter or sweet, and should not eat things harmful to the body even though they are sweet to the palate. In this manner he should conduct himself, and set his heart on being whole and strong, so that his soul be upright to know the Blessed Lord. For it is impossible for a person to understand and grow wise in Torah and commandments while he is ill, or while one of his limbs pains him. Therefore it is not good to fast constantly, lest his strength weaken and his intellect diminish. Therefore he must arrange all his affairs for the service of the Blessed Creator: if he fills his stomach, his body grows heavy; and if he eats too little, he grows weak. And this is good for you: that you eat little of the accompanying dishes, and rely on a single dish as much as you are able, and let a small amount of it suffice for you, as much as you can manage; and let your intent in this be that the bread reach your stomach, not that you indulge yourself. And accustom your soul, at certain times, to do without an accompanying dish altogether, in order to train your nature, so that it will be easy for you at a time you must go without. And if you are able, forgo the accompanying dish altogether, since it involves labor and trouble. And make your eating during the day lighter than your eating at night. And accustom yourself to eat twice a day, so that the movement of your limbs be light during the day, and through this the affairs of your Torah study will be easier for you. And accustom yourself to drink water, unless your intent in drinking wine is for the benefit of your body or to dispel worry; and be very careful not to drink too much of it, for it intoxicates and keeps one far from Torah.
